Affirms the Defense Department's authority to conduct military operations in cyberspace, including clandestine ones and ones short of hostilities, and classifies clandestine military cyber activity as traditional military activity instead of covert action.

::: {.official-links}
**Read the law** (official GovInfo text)

[Enacted text: Pub. L. 115-232](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/plaw/115/public/232){.btn-official} [Current U.S. Code: 10 U.S.C. 394-395](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/10/394?link-type=html){.btn-official}
:::

## Key provisions

- Sec. 394(a)-(b): authority to conduct military cyber activities to defend the United States and its allies, including outside areas of active hostilities.
- Sec. 394(c): a clandestine military cyber operation is a traditional military activity for purposes of the covert action statute.
- Sec. 395: written notice to the armed services committees within 48 hours of a sensitive military cyber operation.
- Related provisions require quarterly cyber operations briefings.

## Why it matters

It settled, in the military's favor, a long interagency argument about whether offensive cyber operations needed a presidential finding. That makes it the clearest statutory marker on the line drawn by the [Intel Oversight Act](intel-oversight-1980.qmd), and its 'short of hostilities' language speaks directly to the [War Powers Resolution](wpr-1973.qmd). It was enacted in [the FY2019 NDAA](ndaa-annual.qmd).

## Current status

In force as enacted by Section 1632 of the FY2019 defense authorization and amended since.

[Last checked November 10, 2026.]{.checked}
